nameStory: The obedient plant earned its charming name from a delightful quirk: if you gently push one of its tubular flowers to the left or right, it will actually stay in that new position like a well-behaved child! This unusual flexibility comes from the flower's hinged attachment to the stem. It's also called false dragonhead because its flowers reminded botanists of the 'true' dragonheads in a different plant genus.
description: Obedient plant is a tall, upright wildflower that can grow 2-4 feet high with a sturdy, square stem typical of the mint family. It produces dense spikes of pink to purple tubular flowers that bloom from bottom to top along the flower head. The plant has a neat, orderly appearance with opposite leaves marching up the stem in pairs. Despite being a native wildflower, it's well-behaved enough to be popular in gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense spikes of pink to purple tubular flowers that you can actually push sideways - they'll stay put! Each flower is about an inch long with a hooded upper lip and spotted lower lip. The flowers open gradually from bottom to top of the spike.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright, 2-4 feet high, with a distinctly square stem that you can feel when you roll it between your fingers. Often grows in small colonies from underground runners.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs up the stem. Leaves have toothed edges and feel slightly rough to the touch. They're attached directly to the stem without stalks.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, small nutlets develop in groups of four at the base of each flower - a classic mint family trait. The dried flower spikes persist into fall and make attractive seed heads.

habitat: Look for obedient plant in moist meadows, prairies, stream banks, and wet ditches throughout New England. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and prefers rich, moist soils but can tolerate some flooding. Often found growing alongside other tall wildflowers like joe-pye weed and ironweed in low-lying areas.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge with square stems and opposite leaves beginning to unfurl. Plants focus on vegetative growth during this season.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from July through August, with tall flower spikes displaying their characteristic pink-purple tubular blooms that open from bottom to top.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but the architectural seed spikes remain standing, turning brown but holding their shape well into autumn. Seeds disperse in late fall.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads may persist above ground, though the plant dies back to underground rhizomes that will produce new shoots in spring.

funFact: Obedient plant flowers have tiny hinges where they attach to the stem, allowing them to bend and stay in whatever position you move them to - making this possibly the only flower you can actually rearrange to your liking for a perfect photo!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tall, spike-flowered plants like purple loosestrife or wild bergamot. The 'push test' is your best friend - if the individual flowers bend and stay put when gently moved sideways, you've found obedient plant! Purple loosestrife has smaller, more numerous flowers that won't budge when pushed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's always well-behaved, obedient plant can actually spread aggressively through underground runners in garden settings, though it's much more restrained in wild conditions. The 'false dragonhead' name reflects old botanical confusion - it was once classified with true dragonheads before getting its own genus.
compareHints: Obedient plant is the only member of its genus Physostegia found in New England, making it unique among our local mint family members. Unlike other mints such as wild bergamot or bee balm that have clustered flower heads, obedient plant's flowers are arranged in neat, orderly spikes. The moveable flowers and tall, unbranched flower spikes distinguish it from all other New England mints.
